passages.text: Leaving Caesarea of Strato, I, Clement, together with Nicetas and Aquila, arrived at Tyre in Phoenicia. At the instruction of Peter, who had sent us, we were received as guests by Berenice, daughter of Justa the Canaanite. She welcomed us most gladly. She exerted herself greatly in the honor she showed me and in her affection for Aquila and Nicetas; in her joy she treated us warmly, speaking freely as though she were an old acquaintance, and hospitably pressed us to care for our bodies. Perceiving, then, that she was allowing us to make a brief postponement, I said, “You do well to hasten to fulfill the duties of love. But fear of our God must be preferred to this. For, since we are engaged in a struggle on behalf of many souls, we are afraid to prefer our own rest to their salvation.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Leaving Caesarea of Strato
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive identifies the city historically; “Strato’s Caesarea” or “Caesarea Stratonis” would also be possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: speaking freely as though she were an old acquaintance
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθης can describe someone familiar or intimate, while παρρησιαζομένη denotes speaking with freedom or frankness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: allowing us to make a brief postponement
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object of the postponement is left implicit in Greek, so the English does not specify whether it was their mission, inquiry, or departure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἡμῶν φόβος
lexical_decisions.chosen: fear of our God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The placement of ἡμῶν naturally permits attachment to θεόν, yielding “our God”; “our fear toward God” remains grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὲρ πολλῶν ψυχῶν τὸν ἀγῶνα ἔχοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: since we are engaged in a struggle on behalf of many souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγών retains the image of a contest or struggle rather than merely denoting responsibility.

passages.text: “We hear that Simon the magician, after being defeated in the debate at Caesarea with our lord Peter, immediately fled and is committing many evils here. For by reviling Peter with every kind of charge contrary to the truth, he sweeps away the souls of the multitude. Though he is a magician himself, he calls that man a magician; though he is a deceiver himself, he publicly denounces that man as a deceiver. And though he himself came off worse in the debates before everyone and fled, he claims to have won. He repeatedly instructs people not to listen to Peter, supposedly out of concern that they might be bewitched by a formidable magician.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς ἐν Καισαρείᾳ πρὸς τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Πέτρον ζητήσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the debate at Caesarea with our lord Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: ζήτησις here denotes a formal dispute or debate. κύριος is retained as the honorific “lord” for Peter rather than being treated as a divine title.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πᾶσι γὰρ τοῖς ὑπεναντίοις παρὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν λοιδορῶν τὸν Πέτρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: by reviling Peter with every kind of charge contrary to the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative plural τοῖς ὑπεναντίοις is taken as substantivized neuter, referring to hostile allegations or means of abuse. A possible alternative is to take it as masculine recipients: “reviling Peter before all his opponents, contrary to the truth.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: deceiver
lexical_decisions.rationale: The word can mean a deceiver, impostor, or one who leads others astray; “deceiver” fits the reciprocal accusation here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: came off worse
lexical_decisions.rationale: This idiom means to emerge as the inferior or defeated party, not literally to carry away something lesser.

lexical_decisions.chosen: supposedly out of concern
lexical_decisions.rationale: δῆθεν marks the stated concern as pretended or merely alleged.

lexical_decisions.chosen: might be bewitched by a formidable magician
lexical_decisions.rationale: δεινός may mean formidable, terrible, or highly skilled; “formidable” preserves the threatening ability implied by Simon’s warning.

passages.text: “Having learned these things, our lord Peter sent us ahead to investigate what had been reported to him, so that, if matters were so, once we had written he himself might learn; and when he comes, he will expose Simon in the very presence of those before whom Simon had slandered him. Since, then, danger involving many souls lies before us, for this reason we have set aside our bodily rest for a little while and wish to learn truthfully from you, since you live here, whether what we have heard is in fact true. So now please tell us every detail.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προἀπέστειλεν ἡμᾶς ἐξεταστὰς τῶν λεχθέντων αὐτῷ ἐσομένους
lexical_decisions.chosen: sent us ahead to investigate what had been reported to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐξεταστάς identifies them as investigators or examiners; the English verbalizes that role without adding a separate office.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once we had written he himself might learn
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek leaves the recipient and contents of the writing implicit, so neither a letter nor a formal report is specified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he will expose Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐλέγχω can mean expose, convict, or refute. “Expose” accommodates both the personal accusations and the anticipated public confrontation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκείνων ἄντικρυς ἐφ’ ὧν αὐτὸν διέβαλλεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the very presence of those before whom Simon had slandered him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκείνων and ὧν are taken as referring to the people before whom Simon had spoken against Peter. The repeated αὐτόν has different contextual referents, made explicit in English to prevent confusion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν ἀναπαύσεως πρὸς βραχὺ ἀμελήσαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: we have set aside our bodily rest for a little while
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμελέω literally means to neglect or disregard; “set aside” expresses the temporary, deliberate forgoing of rest indicated by πρὸς βραχύ.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to learn truthfully
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb denotes learning without falsehood or deception; “reliably” would be another contextual rendering.

passages.text: Having been called upon, Berenice said, “These matters are as you heard. But listen to the other things concerning Simon himself, which perhaps you do not know. For by making apparitions and phantom-images appear in the middle of the marketplace in broad daylight, he astonishes the whole city. When he goes out, statues move and many shadows go before him, which he himself says are the souls of the dead. After quickly reconciling to himself many who were trying to expose him as a sorcerer, he sacrificed an ox under the pretext of a banquet and feasted them, then beset them with various diseases and subjected them to demons. And—to keep from saying too much—after harming many, he has been regarded as a god; besides being fearsome, he has also been held in special honor.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Having been called upon, Berenice said
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although the passive of ἀξιόω can literally mean “having been deemed worthy,” it can contextually introduce someone who has been requested or invited to speak.

lexical_decisions.chosen: apparitions and phantom-images
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired nouns both concern visual manifestations; the differentiated rendering preserves the source’s two terms rather than collapsing them into one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: When he goes out
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle can describe going out, coming forward, or proceeding in public; the surrounding moving statues and preceding shadows suggest a public appearance or procession.

lexical_decisions.chosen: After quickly reconciling to himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαλλάσσω denotes reconciliation or winning people over. εὐθύστερον is rendered “quickly,” though “more readily” or “more directly” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: beset them with various diseases
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιβάλλω literally evokes surrounding or enveloping; with diseases as its instrument, “beset” preserves more of that image than the generic “afflicted.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: subjected them to demons
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποβάλλω here presents the victims as being placed under the power or influence of demons.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τῷ φοβερὸν εἶναι καὶ προτετίμηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: besides being fearsome, he has also been held in special honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: φοβερός actively means fear-inspiring, while the perfect προτετίμηται indicates an established state of exceptional esteem or preference.

passages.text: “Therefore I do not think anyone will be able to extinguish so great a fire once it has been kindled. For no one doubts what that man claims; rather, everyone is firmly convinced that it is so. Therefore, so that you may not be put in danger, I urge you not to attempt anything against him before Peter comes, who alone will be able to contend against so great a power (being the most proven disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ). For I have become so afraid of the man that, if he had not on another occasion also debated with my lord Peter and come off worse, I would have advised you to persuade even Peter himself not to attempt a counter-debate with Simon.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: extinguish so great a fire once it has been kindled
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation retains the explicit metaphor of a fire that has already been ignited.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what that man claims
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπαγγέλλομαι may mean promise, profess, or claim; here it concerns Simon’s asserted powers and representations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: everyone is firmly convinced that it is so
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαβεβαιόομαι can describe emphatic affirmation or settled assurance; the middle form permits the rendering “is firmly convinced.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: against so great a power
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυναστεία can denote power, dominion, or potent authority; “power” best fits Simon’s feared magical capacity in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ δοκιμώτατος ὑπάρχων μαθητής
lexical_decisions.chosen: being the most proven disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοκιμώτατος is superlative and describes one shown to be approved, tested, or proven; the rendering preserves that superlative claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὸν κύριόν μου Πέτρον διαλεχθεὶς τὸ ἧττον ἀπηνέγκατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: debated with my lord Peter and came off worse
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαλέγομαι denotes discussion or debate here, and τὸ ἧττον ἀπηνέγκατο is the idiom for emerging as the defeated or inferior party. “Lord” is lowercased because κύριος is an honorific for Peter in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not to attempt a counter-debate with Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀντεξετάζομαι denotes engaging in examination or disputation in opposition to another; “counter-debate” preserves that reciprocal adversarial force.
